passage: Karthik, sit. I'm Asif, and yes, I overthink flats. The broker first showed me a two-bedroom with a balcony at double my budget, then a one-bedroom that suddenly looked "so reasonable." I nearly signed. Then I remembered how that trick works. I asked myself three things: what is this flat worth by itself, is it better than my old room, and what do I actually need? I work from the office, I cook, I need light. The one-bedroom was cramped and dark. A third place, never shown next to the fancy one, had a big window and a gas line, and it was cheaper too. The other thing: I had been scrolling my college friends' new-home photos every night. I muted them. I'm not living their highlight reel.

qa.q: What did the third flat have?
qa.a: A big window and a gas line.

qa.q: What was happening in Asif's mind when the one-bedroom looked "so reasonable"?
qa.a: Asif was pulled by the contrast with the costly two-bedroom and felt eager to sign, before recognising how that comparison works.

qa.q: Which three questions helped Asif choose, and why do they work?
qa.a: What the flat is worth by itself, whether it beats the old room, and what Asif actually needs; they replace the broker's comparison with Asif's own reference points.

qa.q: What would change if Asif had kept scrolling the friends' new-home photos every night?
qa.a: Every flat might have been measured against their best pictures, making even a good place feel like a failure and the choice harder to trust.

grounding: A young adult judges a flat by its own worth, against their own past and needs, rather than the nearest example or friends' highlight photos.

passage: I'm Charu, Lavanya's flatmate. Last month her school group was all promotions, engagements and beach holidays, and I watched her go quiet after every scroll. One night she put the phone down and started a list on the back of an electricity bill. Left column: "Me, two years ago." Right column: "Me, now." Salary: doubled. Anxiety: much better. Friends: fewer, closer. Cooking: can make biryani. She read it out to me, laughing. Then she added a third column, "What I want next," with only two things: "Learn to drive. Visit Nani in Shillong." She hasn't left the group. She just looks at it less, and when she does, she scrolls quickly and shrugs.

qa.q: What did Lavanya write the list on?
qa.a: The back of an electricity bill.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have been feeling when she went quiet after every scroll?
qa.a: She may have felt discouraged and left behind, measuring her life against her friends' promotions, engagements and holidays.

qa.q: How did the list change what Lavanya compared herself with?
qa.a: She compared herself with who she was two years ago and with what she wants next, instead of her school group's highlights, and saw real progress.

qa.q: How does Charu see the change in Lavanya?
qa.a: Charu notices Lavanya laughing while reading the list and later scrolling quickly and shrugging, though Charu can only watch from outside. 🙂

grounding: A flatmate watches a young woman stop measuring herself against friends' highlights and compare herself with her own past and goals.

passage:
Monday: Vaibhav got a job offer from a small firm in Indore: decent pay, a short commute, a boss who asked good questions. He was pleased, until Indu mentioned that their classmate had just joined a big company in Mumbai. By evening, the offer felt small.
Wednesday: He sat down with Indu and a notebook. "Forget the Mumbai job," she said. "What is this offer worth by itself?" He wrote: "Pay covers rent and savings. Home food. Parents close. I'd learn the whole system, not one small part." Then: "Better than my internship? Much."
Saturday: He accepted. He muted the classmate's office-tour posts for a while, not out of envy, just so the offer could stay the size it really was.

qa.q: Where was the job offer from?
qa.a: A small firm in Indore.

qa.q: Why did the offer feel small by Monday evening?
qa.a: Vaibhav had been pleased, but after hearing about the classmate's big Mumbai job he was measuring his offer against that instead of on its own.

qa.q: Which question from Indu changed the decision on Wednesday?
qa.a: "What is this offer worth by itself?" It made Vaibhav list the offer's own merits and compare it with his internship, not with someone else's job.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt watching the good offer shrink in Vaibhav's eyes?
qa.a: Indu may have felt a bit guilty for mentioning the classmate, and wanted to help him see the offer clearly again.

grounding: Over a week, a young man stops judging a job offer against a classmate's and asks what it is worth by itself and against his own past.

passage: Jomon, you're comparing your salary with your batchmates' posts again. Let your Seema Aunty tell you something. At twenty-five, I had just rented my first flat in Kozhikode, one room, a tiny kitchen, a window facing a wall. That same month, three friends posted photos of new homes: balconies, big sofas, one with a garden. I sat on my plastic chair and felt poor. Then I made myself ask three questions. What is this flat worth by itself? A safe door, my own kitchen, fifteen minutes from work. What was I living in two years ago? A hostel bed with four roommates. What do I actually need? Quiet to study and a stove. Answered like that, it was a good flat. Those photos were their best day, taken from the best angle. My plastic chair was my every day. So, beta, what does your salary do for you, compared with last year?

qa.q: What did Seema Aunty's first flat face?
qa.a: Its window faced a wall.

qa.q: How did Seema Aunty feel when she saw her friends' photos of new homes?
qa.a: She felt poor and discouraged sitting on her plastic chair, because she was comparing her everyday flat with their best-day photos.

qa.q: Which questions helped Seema Aunty, and how could Jomon use them?
qa.a: She asked what the flat was worth by itself, what she had two years ago and what she needed; Jomon could ask what the salary does for Jomon compared with last year.

qa.q: How might the friends who posted the photos have felt about their own posts?
qa.a: They were probably happy to share a good day, without knowing their best-angle photos were making someone else feel poor.

grounding: An aunt tells Jomon how she judged her first flat by its own worth, her own past and her needs rather than against friends' best-day photos.

passage: The scooter showroom in Jaipur closed at eight, the festival discount ended tonight, and Yash, twenty-four, had until then to decide. The salesman had started with the top model: alloy wheels, digital screen, ninety-eight thousand. Next to it, the basic model at sixty-two thousand looked plain and cheap. His friend Tushar's new scooter was all over social media, with a sunset behind it. Yash's sister Aadhya checked her watch. 'Forty minutes.' Yash took a breath and wrote on the back of the brochure. What do I need? Ten kilometres to work, a helmet box, a bit of rain. What was I using before? A cycle and two buses. What is the basic one worth by itself? He read it back. 'The basic one does everything. It's a big step up from buses.' 'And the sunset photo?' Aadhya asked, grinning. 'Tushar's view, not my commute.' He signed for the basic model at 7:52.

qa.q: How far does Yash travel to work?
qa.a: Yash travels ten kilometres to work.

qa.q: Why did the basic scooter first look plain and cheap to Yash?
qa.a: He had just seen the top model with alloy wheels and a digital screen, and Tushar's sunset photos, so the basic one seemed small beside them.

qa.q: Which questions helped Yash choose under time pressure, and why did they work?
qa.a: He asked what he needed, what he used before and what the basic model was worth by itself, which moved the comparison away from the top model and Tushar's photos.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Aadhya seems pleased and amused, seeing him pick what fits his commute instead of chasing Tushar's view.

grounding: Under a deadline a young man judges a scooter by its own worth, his past and his needs, instead of against the costlier model and a friend's highlight photos.

passage:
Leela had been flat-hunting in Pune for three weeks. On Saturday she saw a one-room flat near her office: clean, sunny, a small balcony, ten minutes' walk.
That evening she scrolled Ira's photos from her new two-bedroom flat with a rooftop garden. Suddenly Leela's option looked tiny and sad.
She put the phone down. Then she made herself ask different questions. What would this flat be worth on its own? Compared with her old hostel room, it was huge. Compared with what she needed, a quiet place near work and room for her plants, it was almost perfect.
And Ira's photos? They didn't show Ira's two-hour commute or her rent split with three flatmates.
Leela opened her notes app and wrote: balcony, sun, ten minutes. Then she messaged the landlord.

qa.q: How far was the flat from Leela's office?
qa.a: It was ten minutes' walk.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling after scrolling Ira's photos?
qa.a: Leela felt disappointed and small, as Ira's rooftop garden made her own sunny flat seem tiny and sad.

qa.q: Which questions helped Leela choose, and why?
qa.a: Asking what the flat was worth on its own, against her old hostel room and against her needs, stopped Ira's photos from being the only yardstick.

qa.q: How might Ira's life look different from her photos?
qa.a: Ira's photos didn't show her two-hour commute or sharing rent with three flatmates, so her real life may be less perfect than it looks.

grounding: An adult judges a flat by her own needs and past rather than a friend's curated photos, choosing the reference point deliberately.

passage:
"You got the Chennai offer?" Minakshi said, pouring the tea. "That's amazing!"
"I know." Arohi stirred her cup. "But then I saw Nikita's post. Singapore, rooftop office, free lunches. Mine felt so ordinary next to that."
"Hmm. But is Nikita's life the thing you're choosing between?"
Arohi paused. "No. I'm choosing between this and staying at my current job."
"And compared with that?"
"Compared with that, it's more money, better team, and closer to Amma." She laughed. "It's actually great."
"And Nikita posts her lunches, not her twelve-hour days."
"True." Arohi put her cup down. "Okay. New rule. I compare offers with my real options and what I need. Not with someone's best photos."
"Accept it, then."
"Tonight."

qa.q: Where was Nikita's job?
qa.a: Nikita's job was in Singapore.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling after seeing Nikita's post?
qa.a: Arohi felt deflated, as if her own good offer was ordinary next to Nikita's highlights.

qa.q: Which question from Minakshi changed Arohi's view, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether Nikita's life was really the choice made Arohi compare the offer with her actual alternative and her needs.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel as Arohi decides to accept?
qa.a: Minakshi probably feels happy and a little proud of helping Arohi see the offer clearly.

grounding: An adult compares a job offer with her real alternatives and needs rather than a friend's highlight posts, choosing the reference point deliberately.

passage:
Last winter, when we were planning our wedding, I spent a whole night looking at my cousin Lakshmi's wedding photos. Three days, a palace, a dress that cost more than my car. By morning our small temple ceremony felt like a disappointment.
Then I made a list. Not "what did Lakshmi have?" but "what do we want?" Our families together. Good food. My grandmother well enough to attend, which meant somewhere close. No debt at the end.
Against that list, our plan was perfect. I'd been measuring it against the one wedding I only saw through edited photos, not against what we actually needed.
On the day, my grandmother sat in the front row and cried happy tears. Lakshmi came too, and told me she'd barely slept for a week before hers.
I'm Binita, and I still keep that list.

qa.q: Where did Binita's wedding ceremony take place?
qa.a: It was a small temple ceremony.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling after a night of looking at Lakshmi's photos?
qa.a: Binita felt disappointed, as if the small ceremony was not good enough next to Lakshmi's palace wedding.

qa.q: What did Binita's list help with, and how?
qa.a: The list helped judge the wedding against real wants and needs, like family together and the grandmother attending, instead of against a curated highlight.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see her own wedding compared with Binita's?
qa.a: Lakshmi may see hers as exhausting behind the scenes, since she barely slept for a week before it.

grounding: An adult measures a wedding plan against the couple's own needs rather than a cousin's edited photos, choosing the reference point on purpose.

passage:
Mentoring note, Tuesday. Neelam, career mentor.
Nikita came in upset about her job offer from the Nagpur hospital: a friend from her batch had just posted about a much bigger package in Dubai. For ten minutes she compared salary, city, even the photos of her friend's balcony.
Then she stopped herself. "Wait. That's the wrong ruler." We made two other columns: what she earned last year as a trainee, and what she actually needs: being near her parents, a good training unit, time to study for her exams. Against those, the Nagpur offer looked strong. She also said, "Her balcony photo isn't her whole life."
She accepted the offer on Thursday. Follow-up in three months.

qa.q: Where was Nikita's job offer from?
qa.a: The Nagpur hospital.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she first came in?
qa.a: She felt upset and a little envious, measuring her offer against her friend's much bigger Dubai package.

qa.q: What two comparisons helped Nikita judge the offer?
qa.a: Her own trainee earnings last year and her real needs, like being near her parents and good training.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Nikita's "That's the wrong ruler"?
qa.a: Neelam sees Nikita catching herself and choosing a better reference point, the key step in deciding well.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a young adult choosing her own past and needs as the reference point for a job offer, rather than a friend's highlight post.

passage:
Saturday night.
Seema's engagement photos went up today. Palace hotel, sunset, a ring the size of a chickpea. She'd texted me last week, "Neelam, you're coming to the party na?" By the fifth photo I was sitting on my bed thinking, what am I even doing with my life? One-room flat, nobody special, same job.
Then I did the thing I promised myself. I closed the app and asked: what does my life look like next to MY last year, not Seema's best evening? Last year I was jobless and scared. This year I have a job I like, rent paid on my own, and I finished my first half-marathon.
And the photos are one evening. Last month she told me she's anxious about her in-laws. None of that is in the sunset.
Sent her a heart. Meant it.

qa.q: Where were Seema's engagement photos taken?
qa.a: At a palace hotel, at sunset.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel by the fifth photo?
qa.a: Neelam felt small and discouraged, measuring a whole ordinary life against Seema's best evening.

qa.q: What reference point did Neelam choose instead, and why does it help?
qa.a: Neelam's own last year; it shows real progress, like a new job and a half-marathon, instead of someone's highlights.

qa.q: What might Seema's life look like beyond the photos?
qa.a: Seema has worries too, like feeling anxious about her in-laws, which the sunset pictures don't show.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows switching the comparison from a friend's curated photos to their own past year and needs.

passage: Harish sat on the step of his shop in Mandsaur with the offer letter from the seed company folded in his shirt pocket. Twenty-two thousand a month, field work, a motorbike allowance. His cousin Divyansh, visiting from Indore, had laughed at it over lunch. 'My friend in Bengaluru gets three times that.' Harish had felt small for an hour. Now, alone, he took out a notebook and asked himself different questions. What does the shop bring in a normal month? What did I earn two years ago? What do Amma's medicines and the house need? He wrote two columns. The offer beat the shop and would give him evenings with his daughter. He looked at the Bengaluru figure once more, then crossed it out; that man didn't live in Mandsaur. He signed the letter.

qa.q: What did the seed company offer Harish?
qa.a: Twenty-two thousand a month, field work and a motorbike allowance.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after Divyansh's comment at lunch?
qa.a: Harish felt small and deflated for an hour, because the offer had been set against a big-city salary.

qa.q: What about Harish's approach could someone else use for a big choice?
qa.a: Compare the option with your own past, your real needs and the other options in front of you, rather than with someone else's life far away.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh see the offer differently from Harish?
qa.a: Divyansh measures it against a friend's city salary, while Harish measures it against the shop, his own past and his family's needs in Mandsaur.

grounding: An adult judges a job offer against his own past and needs rather than the nearest flashy example.

passage: Oskar was halfway through a friend's holiday photos when he caught himself sighing at his own Berlin flat: the one radiator, the crooked shelf, the view of the tram depot. Beach in Portugal. Rooftop dinner. New car. His thumb kept moving. He put the phone face down on the table. Elif, his flatmate, looked up from her laptop. 'You've got the face again.' 'Yeah.' He tried something his old football coach used to say: compare yourself with who you were. Two years ago he had been sleeping on his brother's sofa in Hamburg, with no contract. Now he had a job he liked and a room with a door. 'Honestly,' he said, 'this flat is fine. It's not a beach. It isn't meant to be.' Elif grinned and pushed the biscuit tin towards him.

qa.q: Where had Oskar been sleeping two years earlier?
qa.a: On his brother's sofa in Hamburg.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling while scrolling the holiday photos?
qa.a: Oskar felt dissatisfied and a bit envious, sighing at his flat's single radiator and crooked shelf.

qa.q: What small step broke the spell of the photos for Oskar?
qa.a: Putting the phone face down and comparing his life with his own past, not with friends' best moments.

qa.q: How does Elif see Oskar's change of mood?
qa.a: Elif spots 'the face again' and is glad to see him settle; pushing the biscuit tin over shows warmth and relief.

grounding: An adult stops measuring his life against friends' holiday highlights and compares it with his own past instead.

passage: At the nurses' station of the district hospital, Rajni read the transfer notice twice. Day shifts, children's ward, no more night duty. Jaya, eating upma beside her, peered over. 'Paeds? Priya got ICU in Chennai. That's a real career.' Rajni felt the old pinch. Priya's posts were all certificates and rooftop photos. Then she stopped and picked up a pen. Forget Priya, she thought. What do I actually want this year? Sleep. Time for my evening course. Less lifting while my back heals. Better than last year's nights? Yes, by a mile. She wrote 'YES' in the corner of the notice. Jaya raised an eyebrow. 'Just like that?' 'Not just like that,' Rajni said. 'I measured it against me, not against Priya.'

Dear Sudha,
You asked which flat I picked. I nearly chose the one on the ninth floor. After seeing the tiny, dark one first, it looked like a palace. Then I stopped and asked myself: what is it worth by itself? Is it what I need, compared with where I lived last year and what I actually use? Honestly, no. It was far from my office, and I'd be spending two hours a day in traffic. The second flat I saw was smaller but a ten-minute walk away. I also stopped comparing myself to the friends who post their huge living rooms. Those are their best angles, not their lives. I'm signing for the small one on Monday. I think I'll be happy there.
Afreen
